column3: Atomic commit protocol: a coordinator asks every participant to prepare, then tells all to commit or all to abort; blocks if the coordinator fails after prepare.
Backup rule of thumb: 3 copies, on 2 different media, 1 off-site (or in another region/account).
Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability — the guarantees of a database transaction.
A short document recording one decision: context, options, decision, consequences, and when to revisit it.
A cluster of domain objects changed together inside one transaction, with one root that enforces its invariants.
A translation layer that stops another context's model leaking into yours.
Edge component that routes, authenticates, rate-limits and shapes requests for backend services.
One IP address announced from many locations; the network routes each client to the nearest.
Every message is delivered one or more times; consumers must tolerate duplicates.
Every message is delivered zero or one time; losses are possible, duplicates are not.
The fraction of time (or requests) a system serves correctly, often expressed in "nines".
A binary serialization format with reader and writer schemas resolved at read time.
Signalling upstream to slow down when a component cannot keep up, instead of queueing without bound.
Populating a new column or store with historical data, usually in batches alongside live writes.
A backend tailored to one client type (app, web) that aggregates and shapes calls for it.
A compact probabilistic set: "definitely not present" or "probably present", with a tunable false-positive rate.
How many users or systems one failure or bad change can affect.
Running two production environments and switching traffic from the old (blue) to the new (green) at once.
A boundary within which a model and its language are consistent; the unit of ownership in DDD.
Isolating resources (threads, connections, pools) per dependency so one failure cannot exhaust all.
During a network partition a distributed store must choose between consistency and availability.
Sending a small share of traffic to a new version and widening only if its metrics stay healthy.
The application reads the cache, falls back to the database on a miss, and fills the cache itself.
Many requests miss the same expired key at once and overload the source; prevented by locking, coalescing or early refresh.
Streaming a database's committed changes (usually from its log) to other systems.
Edge caches close to users that serve static and cacheable content.
Splitting a system into independent full copies (cells), each serving a subset of users, to bound blast radius.
Deliberately injecting failures in controlled experiments to verify resilience.
Services react to each other's events without a central coordinator.
Stops calling a failing dependency for a while after errors exceed a threshold, then probes before resuming.
The difference between clocks on different machines; why wall-clock timestamps cannot order distributed events safely.
Mapping keys and nodes onto a ring so adding or removing a node moves only a small share of keys.
A bounded set of reused database connections; its size is a key capacity limit.
Kafka consumers sharing a group id divide a topic's partitions among themselves.
How far a consumer is behind the latest message in a partition.
Verifying that a provider still satisfies the requests and responses its consumers depend on (e.g. Pact).
A load-testing error where a stalled system also stalls request sending, hiding the real latency.
A unit-economics metric: infrastructure cost divided by orders served.
Command Query Responsibility Segregation: separate models for writes and for reads.
A conflict-free replicated data type whose replicas can merge concurrent updates deterministically.
Making data unreadable by deleting its encryption key, used for erasure in backups and logs.
A delivery-only warehouse serving quick-commerce orders from a small area.
A requirement that certain data be stored (and sometimes processed) within a given country or region.
A queue that holds messages that repeatedly fail processing, for inspection and replay.
Running a whole distributed system in a simulated, seeded environment so failures can be reproduced exactly.
A lock shared across processes; safe only with leases and fencing tokens.
Services that must be deployed or changed together — the costs of microservices without the independence.
See dead-letter queue.
The Domain Name System, mapping names to addresses through a hierarchy of cached lookups.
A record that something meaningful happened in the domain, named in the past tense.
Recording every money movement as equal debits and credits so balances always reconcile.
Once acknowledged, data survives crashes and failures.
The allowed unreliability under an SLO (e.g. 0.1% of requests); spending it slows releases.
Splitting data into k data and m parity shards so any k of k+m can rebuild it, at lower overhead than replication.
Storing state as the sequence of events that produced it; current state is derived by replay.
A workshop technique that maps a domain by laying out its events on a timeline.
Replicas converge to the same value if updates stop; reads may be stale meanwhile.
Each input affects the output once, achieved by combining at-least-once delivery with idempotency or transactions.
Changing a schema in backward-compatible steps: add the new, migrate, switch, then remove the old.
Moving service from a failed component (e.g. a primary database) to a standby.
One request or event multiplied into many downstream calls or writes — a feed request into feature lookups, or a post into every follower's feed.
A monotonically increasing number checked by the resource, so a stale lock holder's writes are rejected.
An automated check that an architectural property (dependency rules, latency, cost) still holds.
A runtime switch that turns code paths on or off without redeploying.
The weighting or value at which a decision matrix would choose a different option.
Keeping the core function working with reduced features when dependencies fail.
A high-performance RPC framework using HTTP/2 and Protocol Buffers.
One slow item holding up everything behind it on a connection or queue.
A periodic signal that a node is alive, used for failure detection.
Sending a duplicate request after a delay and using whichever answer returns first, to cut tail latency.
Ports and adapters: domain logic at the centre, infrastructure plugged in through interfaces.
A node temporarily stores writes for an unavailable replica and forwards them when it returns.
A probabilistic structure that estimates the number of distinct items in a few kilobytes.
A key or shard receiving a disproportionate share of traffic.
A client-supplied key that lets the server recognise retries and return the original result.
An operation that has the same effect whether applied once or many times.
A rule that must always hold, e.g. "stock never goes below zero".
How much concurrent transactions can see of each other (read committed, repeatable read, serializable).
Randomness added to retry delays so clients don't retry in synchronized waves.
JSON Web Token: a signed, self-contained token carrying claims about a subject.
An ordered, append-only log within a topic; the unit of ordering and parallelism.
Balancing on transport-level connections (L4) versus on application requests such as HTTP (L7).
A logical counter that orders events consistently with causality.
The time to complete one operation, reported as percentiles (p50, p99).
Choosing one node to act as coordinator, typically through consensus or a lease.
A time-limited grant (e.g. a lock) that expires unless renewed.
Every operation appears to take effect instantly at one point between its start and end, in real-time order.
Items in a system = arrival rate × time in system (L = λW).
Rejecting some requests early under overload so the rest succeed.
A log-structured merge tree: writes go to memory and immutable sorted files that are merged in the background.
A query-optimised copy of data, kept up to date from events or changes, that serves reads in CQRS.
A hash tree used to find differing ranges between replicas cheaply.
Independently deployable services organised around business capabilities.
One deployable with strictly enforced internal module boundaries.
Mutual TLS: both client and server authenticate with certificates.
One system serving many customers (tenants) with isolation of data and performance.
Multi-version concurrency control: readers see a snapshot while writers create new row versions.
A tenant or workload consuming shared resources and degrading others.
Understanding a system's internal state from its outputs: metrics, logs and traces.
A delegation protocol for obtaining access tokens; OpenID Connect adds identity on top.
Detecting conflicting updates with a version check at write time instead of locking upfront.
A central coordinator tells services what to do and tracks the workflow.
Writing an event to an outbox table in the same transaction as the business change, then relaying it.
The latency under which 99% of requests complete; the slow tail users notice.
Returning results in pages using a position marker rather than an offset.
The supported, easiest path for building services, adopted because it saves effort.
A family of consensus protocols for agreeing on values despite failures.
The card-industry security standard; scope shrinks when card data never touches your systems.
Restoring a database to any moment by replaying archived logs onto a base backup.
Using different datastores for different access patterns within one system.
A written incident review focused on systemic causes and actions, not individual blame.
A separate queue and worker pool for urgent traffic so bulk work cannot delay it.
Tests that check properties over many generated inputs, shrinking failures to minimal cases.
Protocol Buffers: a binary format whose field numbers enable backward-compatible evolution.
The minimum number of replicas (R, W) that must respond; R + W > N gives overlapping reads and writes.
A consensus algorithm based on an elected leader replicating a log to a majority.
Capping how many requests a client may make per time window.
A copy of the database that serves reads, usually asynchronously updated.
A guarantee that a user sees their own writes immediately.
Comparing records between two systems (e.g. ledger vs settlement file) and resolving differences.
The erasure code used in many storage systems.
How far a replica is behind the primary; bounds stale reads and data loss on failover.
Temporarily holding stock for a checkout until payment succeeds or the hold expires.
Retries from many clients amplifying load on an already failing service.
Matching instance sizes to actual utilisation.
Database-enforced filtering of rows by tenant or user.
Recovery Point Objective (acceptable data loss) and Recovery Time Objective (acceptable downtime).
A sequence of local transactions with compensating actions instead of a distributed commit.
A service storing message schemas and enforcing compatibility rules.
The strongest isolation level: the result equals some serial order of the transactions.
A layer of sidecar proxies handling traffic, security and telemetry between services.
Splitting data across independent database nodes by a shard key.
A helper process deployed next to each service instance (proxy, agent).
Indicator (what you measure), objective (the target), agreement (the contractual promise).
Accepting writes on any reachable nodes during failures, reconciled later.
Two nodes both believing they are the primary and accepting conflicting writes.
Discounted spare cloud capacity that can be reclaimed at short notice.
Sorted String Table: an immutable sorted file of key-value pairs in an LSM tree.
Migrating gradually by routing features one by one from the old system to the new.
Treating concurrent subtasks as one unit with a shared lifetime, cancellation and error handling.
Many waiting clients woken or retrying at once, overwhelming a resource.
Operations completed per unit time.
A rate-limiting algorithm that refills tokens at a fixed rate and allows bursts up to bucket size.
The most frequent items in a stream, often estimated with sketches.
Following a request across services as a tree of timed spans.
See outbox pattern.
Time to live: how long a cached or stored item remains valid.
A reversible decision that can be made quickly; a one-way door deserves more care.
The shared vocabulary of a bounded context, used in both conversation and code.
Cost and value per business unit (per order, per user).
A model of throughput under contention and coherence costs, explaining why adding nodes can reduce throughput.
Per-node counters that detect whether events are causally ordered or concurrent.
Many ring positions per physical node in consistent hashing, to even out load.
Lightweight JVM threads (Project Loom) that make blocking I/O cheap at high concurrency.
Logging changes durably before applying them, so a crash can be recovered by replay.
In stream processing, an estimate that no older event times are still expected.
An HTTP callback from a provider notifying your system of an event.
Caches that update the store synchronously on write, or asynchronously later.
Releasing a new version without making the service unavailable.
Extends CAP: if Partitioned choose Availability or Consistency, Else choose Latency or Consistency.
A map from each term to the documents containing it; the core structure of full-text search.
A standard relevance-scoring function based on term frequency, document frequency and document length.
A prefix tree; each path from the root spells a prefix, which makes prefix lookups fast for autocomplete.
Encoding latitude and longitude into a string whose shared prefixes mean nearby cells.
Counting requests over a rolling time window rather than fixed buckets, avoiding boundary bursts.
A rate limiter that drains requests at a constant rate, smoothing bursts.
A small probabilistic table that estimates item frequencies in a stream, never underestimating.
A 64-bit, roughly time-ordered ID built from a timestamp, a worker id and a sequence number.
Encoding numbers with 0–9, a–z and A–Z, used for short URL codes.
The list of resting buy and sell orders for an instrument, sorted by price and time.
Matching rule: best price first, and among equal prices, the earliest order first.
A time-limited leadership grant; a leader stops acting when its lease may have expired.
A directed acyclic graph of jobs where each runs after its dependencies succeed.
A time-limited URL that lets a client upload or download an object directly from storage.
Uploading a large object in independently retried parts that are assembled at the end.
A site's file stating which paths crawlers may fetch; honouring it is part of polite crawling.
Limiting request rate per host so a crawler does not overload the sites it visits.
The payment provider transferring collected funds to the merchant, usually in daily batches with a report.
A reliability objective for an end-to-end user journey (e.g. checkout), composed from the services it touches.
The undo step for a completed saga step, run when a later step fails.
Situation, Task, Action, Result — the standard structure for behavioural answers (this handbook adds Learning).
A set of prepared, tagged career stories covering the competencies interviewers probe at your level.
Arguing a position with evidence before a decision, then fully supporting the decision once made.
Aligning interviewers' scoring through anchored rubrics and shared review so verdicts are consistent.
A mock interviewer's sheet: prompt, hidden requirements, follow-up chains, curveball, level anchors.
A quick order-of-magnitude calculation of load, storage or bandwidth to guide design choices.
What an interviewer expects at engineer, senior, staff and principal level in scope, depth and judgement.
Reviewing material at growing intervals, timed to just before it would be forgotten.
The scoring dimensions and anchors interviewers use to rate a system design answer.
